report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported. For pregnant people with chronic HBV and **high HBV DNA (≥200,000 IU/mL)**, adding **tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)** in late pregnancy—typically from **28 weeks’ gestation** through delivery—reduces residual mother-to-child transmission when used *in addition to*, not instead of, newborn hepatitis-B vaccination (and hepatitis-B immune globulin where indicated).

The pivotal randomized trial enrolled highly viremic, HBeAg-positive mothers; all infants received immunoprophylaxis, and maternal TDF begun at 30–32 weeks significantly reduced infant HBV infection compared with no maternal antiviral treatment. Evidence is most applicable to high-viremia pregnancies, since newborn immunoprophylaxis alone already prevents most transmission at lower viral loads.

WHO consequently recommends TDF prophylaxis from week 28 until at least birth for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL. Maternal liver indications for ongoing HBV treatment and postpartum monitoring (including possible hepatitis flares after stopping therapy) should be assessed by the treating clinician.
